lessons.title: Common Weeds in Cabbage Fields
lessons.body:
Weeds compete with cabbage for water, nutrients, and sunlight. In Africa, the most common weeds in cabbage fields include blackjack (Bidens pilosa), pigweed (Amaranthus spp.), goosegrass (Eleusine indica), purple nutsedge (Cyperus rotundus), and wandering Jew (Commelina benghalensis). Blackjack has yellow flowers and sticky seeds that cling to clothing; it grows fast and can reduce cabbage yields by up to 40% if not controlled. Pigweed is a broadleaf weed with red stems and small green flowers; it produces thousands of seeds and thrives in fertile soils. Goosegrass is a grassy weed that forms dense mats, especially in compacted soils. Purple nutsedge is a perennial weed with underground tubers; it is very difficult to remove by hand because tubers break off and regrow. Wandering Jew is a creeping weed with blue flowers; it spreads quickly in moist areas and can smother young cabbage seedlings.

To identify these weeds, look at leaf shape, flower color, and growth habit. Blackjack has serrated leaves and yellow flowers. Pigweed has smooth, oval leaves and tiny green flowers. Goosegrass has finger-like seed heads. Purple nutsedge has triangular stems and purple-brown flower heads. Wandering Jew has fleshy stems and blue flowers. Knowing your weeds helps you choose the right control method. For example, purple nutsedge requires repeated cultivation to exhaust tubers, while annual weeds like pigweed are easier to control with mulching or hand weeding.

Scout your cabbage field weekly, especially during the first 4-6 weeks after transplanting, when cabbage is most vulnerable. Walk in a zigzag pattern and note which weeds are present. Keep a simple notebook with dates and weed types. If you see purple nutsedge, act immediately because it spreads fast. Remove weeds before they flower and set seed. A single pigweed plant can produce 100,000 seeds, which will cause problems for years. By identifying weeds early, you can save money on herbicides and labor. Use a hoe or hand pulling for small patches, and consider crop rotation to break weed cycles. Remember, healthy cabbage plants with good spacing and fertility can outcompete some weeds, but you still need to manage them actively.

lessons.title: Mechanical Weed Control Methods
lessons.body:
Mechanical weed control involves using tools and physical effort to remove or destroy weeds. It is the most common method for small-scale cabbage farmers in Africa because it is cheap and does not require chemicals. The main tools are hoes (hand hoe, jembe), machetes, and hand pulling. For cabbage, timely cultivation is critical. Start weeding 2-3 weeks after transplanting, when weeds are small and before they compete with cabbage roots. A sharp hoe is essential; a dull hoe damages cabbage roots and tires you quickly. Hoe shallowly, about 2-3 cm deep, to avoid cutting cabbage feeder roots. Hill soil around cabbage stems to bury small weeds and support the plants.

Hand pulling is best for weeds growing close to cabbage stems, where a hoe might damage the crop. Pull when the soil is moist (after rain or irrigation) because weeds come out easily with roots. For purple nutsedge, hand pulling is not enough because tubers remain; you must dig out the tubers with a fork or hand cultivator. Repeat every 2-3 weeks until cabbage forms a canopy that shades the ground. Once cabbage leaves cover the soil, weed growth slows down.

Mechanical control has advantages: no chemical residues, improves soil aeration, and you can sell or feed some weeds to livestock. But it is labor-intensive. A farmer can weed about 0.1 hectare per day with a hoe. If you have a larger field, consider hiring labor or using a tractor-drawn cultivator. For commercial farms, a tractor with a row crop cultivator can weed between rows, but you must set the tines to avoid damaging cabbage. Always weed before weeds flower; otherwise, you spread seeds. Also, avoid working in wet soil because it compacts the soil and spreads weed seeds. After weeding, remove weed debris from the field to prevent regrowth. Mulching after weeding can suppress new weeds. Combine mechanical control with other methods like crop rotation and mulching for best results. Remember, consistency is key: small, frequent weeding is better than one big weeding session.

lessons.title: Chemical Herbicides and Safe Application
lessons.body:
Chemical herbicides can control weeds in cabbage, but they must be used carefully to avoid crop damage and health risks. In Africa, common herbicides for cabbage include pendimethalin (Stomp), oxyfluorfen (Goal), and glyphosate (Roundup) for pre-planting. Pendimethalin is a pre-emergence herbicide applied before transplanting cabbage; it controls annual grasses and some broadleaf weeds. Oxyfluorfen is also pre-emergence but can be applied after transplanting if cabbage is established. Glyphosate is a non-selective herbicide used before planting to kill existing weeds; it does not leave residue in the soil. Always read the label and follow instructions exactly. Use the correct dose: for pendimethalin, apply 2-3 liters per hectare in 200-300 liters of water. For oxyfluorfen, use 0.5-1 liter per hectare. Overdosing harms cabbage; underdosing fails to control weeds.

Safe application requires protective equipment: gloves, boots, long trousers, long-sleeved shirt, hat, and a face mask. Mix chemicals in a well-ventilated area, away from children and animals. Use a calibrated knapsack sprayer. Calibrate by spraying water on a measured area (e.g., 10 m x 10 m) to see how much water you use, then adjust. Spray in the early morning or late evening when wind is low to avoid drift. Do not spray when it is raining or about to rain. Keep a bucket of soapy water nearby in case of spills. After spraying, wash your hands, face, and clothes thoroughly. Never eat, drink, or smoke while spraying. Store herbicides in a locked cabinet, away from food and feed.

Herbicides can be effective but have drawbacks: they can kill beneficial insects, contaminate water, and leave residues. Use them as a last resort, integrated with mechanical and cultural methods. Rotate herbicides with different modes of action to prevent resistant weeds. For example, do not use only pendimethalin every season; alternate with hand weeding or mulching. Also, note that some weeds like purple nutsedge are not controlled by pendimethalin; you need hand digging or a specific herbicide like halosulfuron. Always check local regulations; some herbicides are banned in certain countries. If you are organic, avoid all synthetic herbicides. Train yourself and your workers on safe use. A simple rule: if you cannot explain the label to someone else, do not use the chemical.

lessons.title: Mulching for Weed Suppression
lessons.body:
Mulching is covering the soil around cabbage plants with organic or inorganic material to block sunlight and prevent weed seeds from germinating. It is one of the most effective and affordable weed control methods for small-scale farmers in Africa. Common organic mulches include dry grass, straw, maize stover, banana leaves, and coffee husks. Inorganic mulches include black plastic film. Apply mulch 2-3 weeks after transplanting, after you have removed existing weeds. Spread a layer 5-10 cm thick around cabbage plants, leaving a small gap (2-3 cm) around the stem to prevent rotting. For organic mulch, you need about 2-3 tons per hectare. For plastic mulch, use black film 30-50 microns thick; it warms the soil and blocks weeds completely. Silver-black plastic also repels aphids.

Mulching has many benefits: it suppresses weeds by 70-90%, conserves soil moisture, moderates soil temperature, and adds organic matter as it decomposes. It also reduces soil erosion and prevents mud splash on cabbage leaves, which lowers disease risk. However, organic mulch can harbor pests like slugs and termites. To reduce this, use dry, clean mulch and avoid thick layers in wet areas. Plastic mulch is more expensive but lasts longer and is easier to apply on larger areas. You can reuse plastic mulch for 2-3 seasons if you handle it carefully. For organic mulch, you may need to add more as it decomposes, especially after heavy rain.

To apply mulch effectively, first weed the field thoroughly. Then lay the mulch evenly between rows and around plants. Do not pile mulch against the cabbage stem; it can cause stem rot. If using plastic, cut holes for cabbage plants and bury the edges to secure it. Mulching works best when combined with other methods. For example, after mulching, you still need to hand-pull any weeds that emerge through the mulch. Also, rotate crops to prevent weed species that tolerate mulch. In dry areas, mulching is a must because it saves water and reduces weeding frequency. A farmer in Kenya reported that mulching with maize stover reduced weeding time from 10 days to 3 days per hectare. Start with a small trial and see the results. Mulch is not a one-time solution; monitor and maintain it throughout the season.

lessons.title: Crop Rotation to Reduce Weed Pressure
lessons.body:
Crop rotation means growing different crops in the same field in a planned sequence. It is a powerful tool to break weed cycles because different crops have different growth habits, planting times, and management practices. Weeds that thrive in cabbage may not survive when you rotate to a different crop. For example, purple nutsedge is a problem in cabbage, but rotating to a dense cover crop like sweet potato or cowpea can shade it out. Similarly, rotating to a cereal like maize allows you to use different herbicides that target broadleaf weeds. In Africa, a good rotation for cabbage is: cabbage â maize â beans â cabbage, or cabbage â sweet potato â groundnuts â cabbage. Each crop should be in the field for one season.

How does rotation reduce weeds? First, it disrupts the life cycle of weeds adapted to cabbage. For instance, blackjack and pigweed are annuals that produce seeds; if you rotate to a crop that is harvested before these weeds set seed, you reduce the seed bank. Second, some crops are more competitive. Maize and sorghum have deep roots and can outcompete weeds for water and nutrients. Third, you can use different weed control methods: in cabbage, you might use hand weeding; in maize, you can use herbicides like atrazine; in beans, you can use close spacing to smother weeds. Fourth, rotating to a legume like beans or groundnuts improves soil fertility, which helps cabbage grow stronger and compete better.

To plan a rotation, know your weeds and your markets. If you have a serious purple nutsedge problem, rotate to a crop that allows repeated tillage, like sweet potato, which can be earthed up to bury nutsedge. Avoid rotating cabbage with other brassicas (e.g., kale, broccoli) because they share pests and weeds. Also, include a fallow period with a cover crop like mucuna or lablab to smother weeds and add organic matter. Keep records of which crops you grow and which weeds appear. After 2-3 years, you will see a reduction in weed pressure. Crop rotation is not a quick fix; it requires planning and patience. But it is cheap, sustainable, and improves overall soil health. Combine rotation with mulching and mechanical weeding for the best results. Remember, no single method controls all weeds; rotation is one part of an integrated strategy.

lessons.title: Integrated Weed Management Strategies
lessons.body:
Integrated Weed Management (IWM) combines multiple methods to control weeds effectively and sustainably. For cabbage, IWM means using mechanical, cultural, chemical, and biological methods together, rather than relying on one. The goal is to reduce weed competition to an acceptable level, not to eliminate all weeds. A good IWM plan starts with prevention: use clean seed, clean tools, and compost that is well-rotted to avoid introducing weed seeds. Then, combine the following practices in a sequence.

First, prepare the land well. Plough and harrow to kill existing weeds. If possible, stale seedbed: prepare the soil, wait 1-2 weeks for weeds to germinate, then shallow cultivate to kill them before transplanting cabbage. This reduces the weed seed bank. Second, transplant healthy cabbage seedlings at the right spacing (60 cm x 45 cm for medium varieties). Close spacing shades the soil faster. Third, apply mulch (organic or plastic) immediately after transplanting. Mulch suppresses 70-90% of weeds. Fourth, hand weed or hoe 2-3 times during the critical period (first 6 weeks). Do this before weeds flower. Fifth, if needed, apply a pre-emergence herbicide like pendimethalin before mulching. But use chemicals sparingly and safely. Sixth, rotate crops each season. For example, follow cabbage with maize, then beans, then cabbage. This breaks weed cycles. Seventh, keep field edges clean; weeds from borders can spread into the field. Eighth, monitor weekly and keep records. If you see a new weed, identify it and act fast.

IWM is more work upfront but saves time and money later. It reduces herbicide use, which lowers costs and health risks. It also improves soil health and cabbage quality. A farmer in Tanzania who used IWM (mulch + hand weeding + rotation) reduced weeding labor by 50% and increased cabbage yield by 30%. Start with a simple plan: for one season, try mulching plus two hand weedings plus rotation. Then adjust based on results. Train your workers on each method. Use local materials for mulch. Share knowledge with neighbors. Remember, weeds are persistent; you must be consistent. IWM is not a one-time fix but a year-round approach. With practice, you will find the right combination for your farm. Always prioritize safe practices and avoid unnecessary chemicals. Healthy cabbage starts with healthy soil and good management.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Integrated Weed Management for Cabbage in Africa

Weed management is one of the most consistent cost centres in African cabbage production. Unlike pests or diseases, weeds are a certainty every season â and in cabbage, they are especially damaging because the crop is slow to establish, has a shallow competitive canopy in the first 3â5 weeks, and is harvested as a fresh market vegetable where cosmetic damage and reduced head size translate directly into lost income. A well-run weed programme in a 1-hectare cabbage plot typically costs 15â25% of total variable costs (largely labour), and poor weed control can reduce marketable yield by 30â60% (FAO, 2022).

This lesson consolidates the six preceding modules into a practical, field-ready reference. It is written for the commercial smallholder and the emerging African agripreneur who needs to plan labour, inputs, and rotations with the same discipline as any other business line item.

Why the First Six Weeks Decide Your Profit

Cabbage yield is largely determined before canopy closure. Research across East and Southern Africa shows that weeds competing during the first 6 weeks after transplanting can reduce head weight by 40â60%, even if the field is kept clean afterwards (FAO, 2022). This is the critical weed-free period. Every weed control decision should be scheduled around it. If you are paying casual labour, that is where the money must go first.

Data Table 1: Common Cabbage Weeds in African Production Systems

Weed Type Why It Matters Primary Control
Amaranthus spp. (pigweed)Broadleaf, annualFast growth, allelopathic, hosts aphidsHand-pull young; mulch; pre-emergence herbicide
Bidens pilosa (blackjack)Broadleaf, annualSticks to harvest, reduces marketabilityEarly hoeing; rotation with cereals
Cyperus spp. (nutgrass)Sedge, perennialDeep tubers, resistant to most hoesRepeated tillage; cover crops; glyphosate spot
Eleusine indica (goosegrass)Grass, annualCompetes for N; hosts cutwormsPre-emergence herbicide; dense spacing
Galinsoga parvifloraBroadleaf, annualRapid seed set, hard to hand-weedMulching; shallow cultivation
Portulaca oleracea (purslane)Broadleaf, annualFleshy stems re-root after hoeingRemove from field; solarisation
Striga spp. (witchweed)ParasiticDrains nutrients; severe in dry zonesRotation with non-host legumes; resistant varieties
Commelina benghalensisBroadleaf, perennialSpreads by stem fragmentsClean tools; repeated cultivation; mulch

Source: FAO (2022), Weed Management in Vegetable Production; CABI (2021), Crop Protection Compendium; AATF (2020), Striga Control in African Farming Systems.

Data Table 2: Comparative Cost and Effectiveness of Weed Control Methods (per hectare, cabbage)

Method Typical Cost (USD/ha) Effectiveness Labour (person-days) Best Fit
Hand weeding (3 rounds)180â350High if timely45â70Small plots, high-value market
Mechanical hoeing (2 rounds)80â150Medium20â35Row-planted, medium scale

Plastic mulch400â700Very high10â15Commercial, dry-season production

Post-emergence herbicide50â100Medium (grass only)5â10Selective grass control

Source: Compiled from FAO (2022); KARI (2019), Cost of Production Survey â Horticulture; and regional agribusiness benchmarks (2023). Costs vary by country and season.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HERBICIDE HANDLING

Herbicides are toxic chemicals. In Africa, paraquat and atrazine misuse has caused serious poisoning. Always: (1) wear gloves, boots, long sleeves, and a face mask; (2) never mix or spray in windy conditions; (3) store chemicals in original labelled containers, locked away from children and food; (4) never eat, drink, or smoke while spraying; (5) wash immediately after application; (6) observe the pre-harvest interval on the label â for cabbage, this is typically 7â21 days depending on product. If poisoning is suspected, contact a clinic immediately and bring the product label. Follow national pesticide registration authority rules (e.g., KEPHIS in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria, DALRRD in South Africa).

Building Your Integrated Weed Management (IWM) Plan

IWM is not a single technique â it is a season-long system that combines prevention, cultural practice, mechanical control, and judicious chemical use. For a commercial cabbage operation, the following sequence gives the best return on investment:

  1. Pre-plant: Deep plough and harrow to expose weed seeds and rhizomes. If Cyperus is present, repeat after 10â14 days. Apply well-rotted manure only â fresh manure introduces weed seeds.
  2. At transplanting: Apply pre-emergence herbicide (e.g., pendimethalin) if labour is scarce, or lay organic mulch between rows. Ensure transplants are sturdy and spaced 45â60 cm apart to close canopy faster.
  3. Weeks 2â3: First hand-weeding or shallow hoeing. Remove weeds before they set seed. This is the highest-value labour you will spend all season.
  4. Weeks 4â6: Second weeding if needed. Spot-treat perennial weeds with a wick applicator or hand-pull. Avoid deep cultivation that damages cabbage roots.
  5. After week 6: Canopy closure suppresses most annual weeds. Hand-pull any escapes before they seed. Do not spray post-emergence herbicides over cabbage unless the label specifically allows it.
  6. Post-harvest: Remove crop residues and weeds. Plant a cover crop (e.g., cowpea, lablab, or cereal rye) to smother weeds and add organic matter.

Crop Rotation: The Cheapest Long-Term Weapon

Continuous cabbage on the same land selects for the same weed spectrum and builds up soil-borne problems. A 3â4 year rotation with cereals (maize, sorghum, millet), legumes (beans, cowpea, groundnut), or root crops (sweet potato) breaks weed cycles, especially for Striga and Cyperus. In East Africa, rotating cabbage with maize + beans has been shown to reduce weed biomass by 35â50% in the following cabbage crop (AATF, 2020). For the business-minded farmer, rotation also improves soil fertility, reducing fertiliser bills.

Mulching: A Dual-Purpose Investment

Organic mulch (dry grass, straw, maize stover) applied 5â8 cm thick between rows suppresses 70â90% of annual weeds, conserves soil moisture, and moderates soil temperature. In dry-season cabbage production in Kenya, Tanzania, and Nigeria, mulch often pays for itself through reduced irrigation and weeding costs. Plastic mulch (black or silver) is more expensive but gives near-total weed suppression and is standard in commercial export operations. Silver mulch also repels aphids and thrips, adding a pest-control benefit.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Scout weekly â identify weeds before they flower or set seed.
  • â Protect weeks 0â6 â this is the critical weed-free period; never skip it.
  • â Use clean seed, tools, and manure â prevention is cheaper than control.
  • â Combine at least 3 methods â mulch + hand-weeding + rotation, or herbicide + hoeing + mulch.
  • â Rotate away from cabbage for at least 2 seasons with cereals or legumes.
  • â Train and equip workers â correct herbicide mixing, PPE, and safe disposal.
  • â Record costs and yields â know your cost per weeding round and return per hectare.
  • â Remove weeds from the field â never leave pulled weeds on the beds; they re-root or shed seed.
  • â Check pre-harvest intervals â a residue violation can destroy your market access.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Weed Management in Vegetable Production (2022)
  • CABI Crop Protection Compendium â Brassica oleracea
  • AATF â Striga Control in African Farming Systems (2020)
  • KEPHIS Kenya â Pesticide Registration and Safe Use Guidelines
  • IITA â Integrated Weed Management for Smallholder Farmers

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme â Cabbage Farming. Always verify chemical registrations and pre-harvest intervals with your national regulator before use.

quiz.q: Which weed is a perennial with underground tubers that is very difficult to control by hand pulling?
quiz.explanation: Purple nutsedge has tubers that break off and regrow, making hand pulling ineffective.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for hoeing to avoid damaging cabbage roots?
quiz.explanation: Shallow hoeing of 2-3 cm avoids cutting cabbage feeder roots.

quiz.q: Which herbicide is a pre-emergence herbicide commonly used in cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Pendimethalin (Stomp) is applied before transplanting to control annual weeds.

quiz.q: How thick should an organic mulch layer be for effective weed suppression?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of organic mulch blocks sunlight and suppresses weeds.

quiz.q: Which crop rotation sequence is recommended to reduce weed pressure in cabbage?
options: A) Cabbage â cabbage â cabbage
B) Cabbage â maize â beans â cabbage
C) Cabbage â kale â broccoli â cabbage
D) Cabbage â fallow â cabbage
quiz.explanation: Rotating with maize and beans breaks weed cycles and improves soil fertility.

quiz.q: What is the first step in an Integrated Weed Management plan?
options: B) Use clean seed and tools
quiz.explanation: Prevention by using clean seed and tools avoids introducing weed seeds.

quiz.q: Which weed produces thousands of seeds and thrives in fertile soils?
quiz.explanation: Pigweed (Amaranthus) produces up to 100,000 seeds per plant.

quiz.q: When is the best time to hand pull weeds?
options: C) After cabbage forms a canopy
quiz.explanation: Weeds come out easily with roots when soil is moist after rain or irrigation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of pendimethalin per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Apply 2-3 liters of pendimethalin in 200-300 liters of water per hectare.

quiz.q: Which protective equipment is NOT essential when applying herbicides?
quiz.explanation: Sandals do not protect feet; boots are required for safe herbicide application.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching with black plastic film?
options: B) It warms the soil and blocks weeds
quiz.explanation: Black plastic mulch warms soil and provides complete weed suppression.

quiz.q: How does crop rotation reduce weed pressure?
options: A) It kills all weeds instantly
B) It disrupts weed life cycles
quiz.explanation: Different crops and management practices break weed cycles and reduce seed banks.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mechanical weed control method?
quiz.explanation: A hoe is a mechanical tool used to remove or destroy weeds.

quiz.q: What is the critical period for weed control in cabbage?
options: B) After cabbage forms a canopy
quiz.explanation: Cabbage is most vulnerable to weed competition in the first 4-6 weeks.

quiz.q: Which weed has yellow flowers and sticky seeds?
quiz.explanation: Blackjack (Bidens pilosa) has yellow flowers and sticky seeds that cling to clothing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for cabbage to help shade out weeds?
quiz.explanation: 60 cm x 45 cm is a common spacing for medium cabbage varieties, promoting canopy closure.

quiz.q: Which herbicide is non-selective and used before planting?
quiz.explanation: Glyphosate kills all existing weeds before planting and leaves no soil residue.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of organic mulch?
options: C) It can harbor pests like termites
quiz.explanation: Organic mulch can provide habitat for pests such as termites and slugs.

quiz.q: Which crop is a good rotation partner for cabbage to smother purple nutsedge?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato forms a dense canopy and allows repeated tillage that can bury nutsedge tubers.

quiz.q: What is the stale seedbed technique?
options: A) Planting cabbage immediately after ploughing
B) Preparing soil, waiting for weeds to germinate, then shallow cultivating
quiz.explanation: Stale seedbed reduces weed seed bank by killing germinated weeds before transplanting.

quiz.q: How often should you scout for weeds in cabbage?
options: D) Only when weeds are tall
quiz.explanation: Weekly scouting helps identify weeds early and plan timely control.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gap between mulch and cabbage stem?
quiz.explanation: A 2-3 cm gap prevents stem rot from excess moisture.

quiz.q: Which weed has triangular stems and purple-brown flower heads?
quiz.explanation: Purple nutsedge is identifiable by its triangular stems and purple-brown flower heads.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of integrated weed management?
options: B) Reduces labor and costs over time
quiz.explanation: IWM combines methods to reduce labor, herbicide use, and costs while improving yields.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing weeds close to cabbage stems?
quiz.explanation: Hand pulling avoids damaging cabbage roots and stems when weeds are very close.

quiz.q: How much can mulching reduce weeding time according to a Kenyan farmer example?
options: A) From 10 days to 3 days per hectare
B) From 3 days to 10 days per hectare
C) From 5 days to 1 day per hectare
quiz.explanation: Mulching with maize stover reduced weeding time from 10 days to 3 days per hectare.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to calibrate a knapsack sprayer?
options: A) Spray water on a measured area and measure usage
C) Fill to the top and spray until empty
D) Use the same setting for all chemicals
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures you apply the correct dose by measuring output on a known area.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a component of integrated weed management?
options: C) Using only one herbicide every season
quiz.explanation: Relying on one herbicide leads to resistant weeds; IWM uses multiple methods.

quiz.q: What should you do with weed debris after mechanical weeding?
options: A) Leave it in the field
B) Remove it from the field
quiz.explanation: Removing weed debris prevents regrowth and seed spread.

quiz.q: Which crop is a legume that can be included in rotation to improve soil fertility?
quiz.explanation: Beans fix nitrogen and improve soil fertility, benefiting subsequent cabbage crops.
